ImageDescription.value: The final chapter in a remarkable mission of exploration and discovery, Cassini's Grand Finale is in many ways like a brand new mission. Twenty-two times, NASA's Cassini spacecraft will dive through the unexplored space between Saturn and its rings. What we learn from these ultra-close passes over the planet could be some of the most exciting revelations ever returned by the long-lived spacecraft. This animated video tells the story of Cassini's final, daring assignment and looks back at what the mission has accomplished. The Cassini mission is a cooperative project of NASA, ESA (the European Space Agency) and the Italian Space Agency. The Jet Propulsion Laboratory, a division of the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, manages the mission for NASA's Science Mission Directorate, Washington. For more information about Cassini's Grand Finale, please visit https://saturn.jpl.nasa.gov/grandfinale.

144904872.title: File:Crowd at Tony Evers' 2022 election night party react to CNN's projection of Evers' victory.webm

ObjectName.value: Crowd at Tony Evers' 2022 election night party react to CNN's projection of Evers' victory

Categories.value: CNN|Self-published work|License review needed (video)|Uploaded with video2commons|Tony Evers' 2022 election night party

ImageDescription.value:
Crowd at Tony Evers' 2022 election night party (held at the Orpheum Theatre in Madison, Wisconsin) reacts to CNN's projection of Evers' victory. For nearly all in the room, this projection was the first confirmation that Evers would indeed be reelected. Since CNN was the only network which the video screen at the party was showing, this was the first that many there had seen that Evers would indeed be reelected.

Another major network (either ABC or NBC/MSNBC) had made their call shortly before this and Evers' Republican challenger Tim Michels had already conceded, though CNN had not yet reported on Michels' concession (since I and others near me were following news on our phone, we were awar of both the other networks' call and Michels' concession, and this was the reason I hit record quickly after CNN's graphics indicated they would be making a breaking projection, as I correctly expected it would be on the Wisc. governors race).

Credit.value: Own video

ObjectName.value: Discover the first ever image of a black hole

Categories.value: Videos from YouTube|Videos of 2019|Uploaded with video2commons|License reviewed by YouTubeReviewBot|Videos of black holes

ImageDescription.value:
EU-funded scientists have contributed to a major astronomical discovery: the capturing of the first ever image of a black hole. The discovery is the result of an international science collaboration called Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) that linked several observatories across the globe and some 200 researchers in Europe, the US and East Asia. A grant from the European Research Council allowed three European scientists to play a key role in this discovery: Professors Heino Falcke, Professor of Astroparticle Physics and Radio Astronomy at the Radboud University Nijmegen, Luciano Rezzolla, Director at the Institute for Theoretical Physics (ITP) of the Goethe University of Frankfurt, Michael Kramer, Director at the Max-Planck-Institut für Radioastronomie (MPIfR) in Bonn.

Categories.value: Self-published work|Number 312 on rail vehicles|Number 9 on rail vehicles|Number 10 on rail vehicles|Level crossings in Utah|Utah Transit Authority in 2016|June 2016 in Utah|2016 in Provo, Utah|Provo Central station|Videos of the FrontRunner|Bombardier BiLevel coaches of the FrontRunner|MPI MP36PH-3C locomotives of the FrontRunner|Pullman-Standard Comet I cars of the FrontRunner|Photographs by An Errant Knight|2016 Warriors Over the Wasatch

ImageDescription.value: For the first time ever, the Utah Transit Authority's (UTA) FrontRunner provided Sunday fare service (not including late, late Saturday night service) when a train pulled out of the Provo station at 5:55 am on Sunday 26 June 2016. According to UTA, an unidentified third party subsidized the service such the it was able to provide very limited Sunday service at regular fare to assist with transportation to the Warriors Over the Wasatch airshow at Hill Air Force Base. The service was limited to just three trains in each direction in the morning (from the Provo and Ogden station to the Clearfield station) and three more trains in the late afternoon (from Clearfield to Ogden and Provo). UTA also provided shuttle service between the Clearfield station and the airshow on the base. According to the Deseret News, attendance was anticipated to exceed 300,000 each of the two days of the airshow (Saturday and Sunday).

162052980.title: File:Rosetta’s ever-changing view of a comet ESA383716.webm

ObjectName.value: Rosetta’s ever-changing view of a comet ESA383716

Categories.value: CC-BY-SA-3.0-IGO|Content created by the European Space Agency|Uploaded with video2commons|Video display resolution 1920 x 1080|ESA files uploaded by OptimusPrimeBot|Photos of Comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko taken by Rosetta

ImageDescription.value:
These 210 images reflect Rosetta’s ever-changing view of Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko between July 2014 and September 2016.
The sequence begins in the month leading up to Rosetta’s arrival on 6 August, when the comet was barely a few pixels in the field of view. Suddenly, the curious shape was revealed and Rosetta raced to image its surface, coming within 10 km, to find a suitable place for Philae to land just three months later.
Philae’s landing is featured with the ‘farewell’ images taken by both spacecraft of each other shortly after separation, and by Philae as it drew closer to the surface at its first touchdown point. An image taken at the final landing site is also shown.
The subsequent images, taken by Rosetta, reflect the varying distance from the comet as well as the comet’s rise and fall in activity as they orbited the Sun.
Before the comet reached its most active phase in August 2015, Rosetta was able to make some close flybys, including one in which the lighting geometry from the Sun was such that the spacecraft’s shadow could be seen on the surface.
Then, owing to the increase of dust in the local environment, Rosetta had to maintain a safer distance and carry out scientific observations from afar, but this also gave some impressive views of the comet’s global activity, including jets and outburst events.
Once the activity began to subside, Rosetta could come closer again and conduct science nearer to the nucleus, including capturing more high-resolution images of the surface, and looking out for changes after this active period.
Eventually, as the comet returned to the colder outer Solar System, so the available solar power to operate Rosetta fell. The mission concluded with Rosetta making its own dramatic descent to the surface on 30 September 2016, the final images taken reflected in the last images shown in this montage.
Explore thousands of Rosetta images in our Archive Image Browser.
More about Rosetta and its science discoveries.

196840764.title: File:This is the best video I've ever seen.webm

ObjectName.value: This is the best video I've ever seen

Categories.value: Videos from YouTube|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 missing SDC copyright license|Creative Commons Attribution missing SDC copyright status|Uploaded with video2commons|Videos of 2026|Videos in American English|Videos taken on 2026-07-20

ImageDescription.value:
In today's video, I react to police bodycam footage showing an encounter that quickly spiraled out of control after an officer referred to an individual as "he" instead of "she."

What could have been a simple interaction immediately turned into an emotional confrontation. Rather than calmly correcting the officer or moving on with the conversation, the individual repeatedly screamed at the top of his lungs, interrupted the officers, and refused to cooperate throughout the encounter.

The bodycam footage shows the officer exercising a considerable amount of patience. Instead of immediately escalating the situation, he repeatedly instructed the individual to calm down, stop yelling, and comply with lawful commands. At one point, the officer even warned that the behavior needed to stop while making it clear he was prepared to use pepper spray if necessary.

Despite multiple opportunities to de-escalate, the individual continued yelling and refusing to comply.

Eventually, the officer made the decision to place him under arrest.

The situation serves as a reminder that police encounters are not debates over who can yell the loudest. Whether someone believes an officer made a mistake or used the wrong pronoun, screaming, refusing lawful commands, and escalating the encounter is rarely going to improve the outcome. Remaining calm and addressing disagreements through the appropriate channels is almost always the safer approach.

One of the biggest problems with modern social media culture is that some people have been encouraged to believe every personal disagreement is a public moral battle. Not every misunderstanding is an attack, and not every interaction needs to become a viral confrontation. Sometimes the most effective response is simply correcting someone respectfully and continuing the conversation.

The footage also highlights the importance of complying with lawful police instructions during an encounter. If someone believes an officer acted improperly, there are legal processes, complaint procedures, and courts designed to address those concerns. Turning a routine interaction into a disorderly confrontation generally only creates additional legal problems.

In this video, I react to the bodycam footage, discuss why personal disagreements should never become excuses for disorderly conduct, and explain why respecting lawful police orders benefits everyone involved.

Because thinking the rules don't apply to you...

...is often the fastest way to make a bad situation even worse.

Let me know what you think in the comments. Do you think too many people escalate routine interactions with police over issues that could be handled calmly?

ImageDescription.value:
Astronomers using ESO’s Very Large Telescope (VLT) have detected a stellar-mass black hole much further away than any other previously known. With a mass twenty times that of the Sun, this is also the second most massive stellar mass black hole ever found. The newly announced black hole lies in a spiral galaxy called NGC 300, six million light-years from Earth.
This video zooms in onto the position of the system containing the stellar-mass black hole, and finishes with an artist’s impression of the system.
